title: Global Traffic Routing and Health Check Failover with Amazon Route 53
goal: Configure Amazon Route 53 health checks and a failover routing policy to automatically reroute global user traffic away from an unhealthy primary endpoint to a healthy secondary endpoint. Understand how TTL and DNS caching affect failover timing.
flow: Configure Route 53 health checks for primary and secondary endpoints
Create failover routing records with appropriate TTL
Verify DNS failover to secondary endpoint
Understand TTL and DNS caching impact on RTO
Clean up health checks, records and hosted zone

concepts.title: Failover Routing Policy
concepts.body: Route 53 failover routing policy designates one record as primary and another as secondary. When the primary health check fails, Route 53 returns the secondary record.

concepts.title: Health Checks
concepts.body: Route 53 health checks monitor endpoints (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP) or other Route 53 health checks (calculated). They run from multiple AWS locations globally.

concepts.title: TTL and DNS Caching
concepts.body: DNS records have a Time To Live (TTL) value in seconds. Resolvers and clients cache records for this duration. Lower TTLs reduce failover time but increase DNS query costs. DNS failover is not instantaneous.

concepts.title: Evaluate Target Health
concepts.body: When enabled on alias records, Evaluate Target Health allows Route 53 to follow health checks of the target resource (e.g. load balancer targets) rather than requiring a separate health check.

concepts.title: RTO vs TTL
concepts.body: The effective Recovery Time Objective (RTO) for DNS failover is influenced by the health check interval, failure threshold, and the TTL of the DNS record. Lower TTL and shorter health-check intervals reduce effective RTO.

whyItMatters: Route 53 is the primary DNS-layer mechanism for achieving global high availability and disaster recovery failover on AWS. Understanding health checks, failover routing policies, and TTL is essential for SAA-C03 architecture questions. DNS failover is not instantaneous — TTL and resolver caching affect how quickly clients see the new record.

values.label: DNS TTL
values.value: Lower values (e.g. 60s) speed up failover at higher query cost

costWarning: Route 53 hosted zone, DNS query, health-check and traffic-routing charges may apply.

consoleSteps.title: Set up the lab user and permissions

instructions.text: Sign in to the AWS Management Console.
Use an IAM user or role (do not use the root user).
For least privilege, use the grouped permissions below.

consoleSteps.note:
Identity check:
sts:GetCallerIdentity Route 53 permissions:
route53:CreateHostedZone, route53:CreateHealthCheck, route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets Cleanup:
route53:DeleteHealthCheck, route53:DeleteHostedZone
consoleSteps.warning: Do not leave broad admin access or long-term access keys in real company accounts.

consoleSteps.title: Create Route 53 Health Check for Primary Endpoint

instructions.text: Open Amazon Route 53 Console -> Choose Health checks -> Click Create health check.
Set Name to primary-endpoint-healthcheck.
Select What to monitor Endpoint -> Protocol HTTP -> Domain name or IP of Primary ALB.
Set Path to / -> Failure threshold to 3 -> Click Next -> Click Create health check.

consoleSteps.note: Route 53 probes the primary endpoint globally every 30 seconds.

consoleSteps.title: Configure Primary Failover Record (Active)

instructions.text: Open Route 53 Console -> Choose Hosted zones -> Select your domain.
Click Create record.
Set Record name to app.example.com -> Select Routing policy Failover.
Set Failover record type to Primary.
Toggle Alias to Yes -> Route traffic to Alias to Application and Classic Load Balancer -> Select us-east-1 Primary ALB.
Under Health check ID, select primary-endpoint-healthcheck.
Click Create records.

consoleSteps.note: Primary record serves 100% of traffic as long as the health check remains healthy.

consoleSteps.title: Configure Secondary Failover Record (Passive)

instructions.text: Click Create record.
Set Record name to app.example.com -> Select Routing policy Failover.
Set Failover record type to Secondary.
Toggle Alias to Yes -> Route traffic to eu-west-1 Secondary ALB.
Set Record ID to Secondary-Passive.
Click Create records.

consoleSteps.note: Secondary record acts as the passive backup target during primary outages.

consoleSteps.title: Simulate Primary Failure and Test Automatic DNS Failover

instructions.text: Block traffic or stop web service on Primary ALB to trigger health check failure.
Monitor Route 53 Health Check status -> Confirm status transitions to Unhealthy.
Perform DNS lookup: dig app.example.com (or nslookup app.example.com).
Confirm Route 53 DNS responses automatically resolve to the Secondary ALB endpoint IP address.

consoleSteps.note: Validates automatic Active-Passive DNS failover routing.

consoleSteps.title: Tear down lab resources

instructions.text: Delete resource record sets in hosted zone.
Delete health check primary-endpoint-healthcheck.
Delete test hosted zone.

consoleSteps.warning: Delete health checks and record sets before deleting hosted zones.

cliSteps.title: Check your AWS identity
cliSteps.note: Expected: account ID and IAM user/role ARN.
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: account ID and IAM user/role ARN.

verification.text: Confirm Route 53 health checks show Healthy status for the primary endpoint.
Confirm DNS failover records exist for both primary and secondary endpoints with correct TTL.
Confirm that simulating a primary failure triggers Route 53 to route traffic to the secondary endpoint.

cleanup.text: Delete all test Route 53 health checks created for this lab.
Remove the failover DNS records (primary and secondary) from the hosted zone.
Delete the hosted zone only if it was created solely for this lab.
Delete CloudWatch alarms and SNS notifications created for health-check monitoring.

cheatSheet.title: Failover Record Setup
cheatSheet.body: Create a Primary FAILOVER record pointing to your active endpoint with a health check. Create a Secondary FAILOVER record pointing to your DR endpoint. Enable health checks on the primary.

cheatSheet.title: Health Check Types
cheatSheet.body: Endpoint health checks: monitor a URL or IP. Calculated health checks: combine results of multiple child health checks. CloudWatch alarm health checks: based on a CloudWatch alarm state.

cheatSheet.title: TTL Best Practice
cheatSheet.body: Lower TTL before a planned failover or maintenance window. Restore normal TTL afterward to reduce DNS query costs.

troubleshooting.title: Health Check Shows Unhealthy Unexpectedly
troubleshooting.body: Check that security groups and NACLs allow inbound connections from Route 53 health check IP ranges. Verify the endpoint is responding correctly on the configured port and path.

troubleshooting.title: Failover Not Happening
troubleshooting.body: Verify the primary record has a health check associated. Check that Evaluate Target Health is enabled if using alias records. Confirm the health check is actually failing.

troubleshooting.title: DNS Still Resolving to Old Endpoint
troubleshooting.body: DNS caching at the resolver or client level based on TTL. Wait for the TTL to expire. Use tools like dig or nslookup to check current DNS responses from multiple locations.

examTraps.title: DNS Failover Is Not Instantaneous
examTraps.body: TTL and resolver caching mean clients may continue resolving to the failed endpoint for the TTL duration even after health check failure is detected. This must be factored into RTO calculations.

examTraps.title: Private Hosted Zones and Health Checks
examTraps.body: Route 53 health checks cannot directly monitor VPC-internal endpoints. Use CloudWatch alarm-based health checks for internal resources.

examTraps.title: Failover vs Weighted vs Latency Routing
examTraps.body: Failover routing is for active-passive DR. Weighted routing splits traffic by percentage. Latency routing directs users to the lowest-latency region. Do not confuse them.

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Route 53 failover routing requires a health check on the primary record. When the health check fails, Route 53 returns the secondary record. TTL and resolver caching affect how quickly clients see the change.
SAA-C03: Failover routing is for active-passive DR. For active-active with health-based distribution, consider weighted or latency routing with health checks.

memoryHook: Route 53 failover = DNS-layer lifeguard. When primary drowns (health check fails), secondary gets the traffic — but clients cached to the old answer still need to wait for their TTL to expire.

title: Implementing Disaster Recovery Tiers: Pilot Light and Warm Standby
goal: Evaluate Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) trade-offs across the four AWS disaster recovery strategies: backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active. Design and simulate a pilot light and warm standby configuration for a representative workload.
flow: Understand RTO and RPO definitions and how they relate to business requirements
Compare the four DR strategies on cost, RTO and RPO
Design a pilot light configuration for a sample workload
Design a warm standby configuration for the same workload
Simulate a regional failure and describe recovery steps

concepts.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
concepts.body: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption. It is a business requirement, not an automatic guarantee. Lower RTO requires more expensive architectures.

concepts.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
concepts.body: RPO is the maximum acceptable data-loss window, measured in time before the failure. Lower RPO requires more frequent backups or synchronous replication. Asynchronous cross-region replication does not provide zero RPO.

concepts.title: Backup and Restore
concepts.body: The lowest-cost strategy. Infrastructure may need to be fully recreated after a disaster. RTO and RPO are typically the highest of the four strategies. Restore procedures must be tested regularly.

concepts.title: Pilot Light
concepts.body: Core services (such as a minimal database replica or AMI) remain running at minimal scale. Other resources are provisioned during recovery. Provides lower RTO than backup-and-restore at moderate cost.

concepts.title: Warm Standby
concepts.body: A scaled-down but fully functional environment runs continuously. Recovery involves scaling up capacity. Provides faster RTO than pilot light at higher ongoing cost.

concepts.title: Multi-Site Active-Active
concepts.body: Multiple full-scale production environments actively serve traffic simultaneously. Provides the lowest RTO (near-zero) and RPO at the highest cost and operational complexity. Requires data replication and conflict resolution.

whyItMatters: The SAA-C03 exam tests your ability to select the appropriate DR strategy based on RTO and RPO requirements and cost constraints. Understanding the four strategies and their trade-offs is a core architectural skill. Asynchronous replication across regions does not guarantee zero RPO — data in transit may be lost during a regional failure.

values.label: Pilot Light RTO/RPO
values.value: Moderate (tens of minutes) / Lower data-loss risk

costWarning: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region architectures can create charges for duplicate compute, storage, networking, data transfer, load balancing and monitoring resources. Pilot light and warm standby environments incur ongoing costs for their running resources.

instructions.text: Review AWS 4 disaster recovery strategy evaluation framework.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Tier 1: Backup & Restore Architecture

instructions.text: Use Backup & Restore when business requires lowest cost and can tolerate hours/days of downtime.
Store S3 cross-region replication backups and CloudFormation infrastructure templates.

consoleSteps.note: Highest RTO/RPO with lowest operational cost.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Tier 2: Pilot Light Architecture

instructions.text: Use Pilot Light when database must be continuously replicated, but compute servers can remain stopped or as Launch Templates until failover.
On failover, start EC2 instances and scale ASG to full capacity.

consoleSteps.note: Keeps core data burning (database) while compute is dormant.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Tier 3: Warm Standby Architecture

instructions.text: Use Warm Standby when business requires minutes of RTO and can afford running a scaled-down mini version of the full stack continuously.
On failover, scale Auto Scaling Group from min=1 to full production capacity.

consoleSteps.note: A minimal environment is always live in the DR region.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Tier 4: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture

instructions.text: Use Multi-Region Active-Active for mission-critical applications requiring sub-second RTO and RPO.
Deploy DynamoDB Global Tables or Aurora Global Database across multiple active regions.

consoleSteps.note: Lowest RTO/RPO at highest operational cost.

consoleSteps.title: Review SAA-C03 DR Decision Matrix Rules

instructions.text: Verify scenario criteria matching RTO/RPO constraints against DR tier choices.

consoleSteps.note: Guarantees 100% accuracy on DR exam questions.

cheatSheet.title: DR Strategy Comparison
cheatSheet.body: Backup & Restore: lowest cost, highest RTO/RPO. Pilot Light: core runs, medium cost. Warm Standby: reduced environment runs, lower RTO. Multi-site Active-Active: all runs, lowest RTO, highest cost.

cheatSheet.title: RTO vs RPO
cheatSheet.body: RTO = How long can you be down? RPO = How much data can you lose? Both are business decisions, not technical defaults.

cheatSheet.title: Async Replication Caveat
cheatSheet.body: Cross-region async replication (Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 CRR) provides near-zero RPO but not zero RPO. In-flight data may be lost during a regional failure.

troubleshooting.title: Confusing Pilot Light and Warm Standby
troubleshooting.body: Pilot light: only minimal core services run (e.g. a stopped RDS instance or minimal replica). Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully operational environment runs. The key difference is whether the secondary is operational or just seeded.

troubleshooting.title: Async Replication Zero-RPO Claim
troubleshooting.body: Asynchronous replication (e.g. Aurora Global Database secondary) is not zero RPO. There is always a replication lag. Synchronous replication (e.g. RDS Multi-AZ within a region) is closer to zero RPO for AZ failures but not cross-region.

examTraps.title: DR ≠ HA
examTraps.body: High availability reduces downtime during partial failures (e.g. AZ failure). Disaster recovery restores service after a major failure. They are complementary but distinct concepts.

examTraps.title: Asynchronous Cross-Region Replication Is Not Zero RPO
examTraps.body: The SAA exam may offer "use Cross-Region Replication for zero RPO" as a trap. Asynchronous replication always has some lag. Only synchronous writes (rare cross-region) could achieve near-zero RPO.

examTraps.title: Backup-and-Restore Is Not Just Snapshots
examTraps.body: Backup-and-restore requires restoring the snapshot AND recreating or reconfiguring the surrounding infrastructure. Test the full restore process, not just snapshot creation.

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Know the four DR strategies in order of cost and RTO/RPO: Backup & Restore (cheapest, slowest) → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Multi-site Active-Active (most expensive, fastest).
SAA-C03: RTO and RPO are business requirements. AWS services and architectures can achieve them, but AWS does not automatically guarantee any specific RTO or RPO value.
SAA-C03: Cross-region asynchronous replication (Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 CRR) does not provide zero RPO. In-transit data may be lost during a regional failure.

memoryHook: DR tiers = Cost vs speed trade-off. Backup-and-Restore is cheapest but slowest. Pilot Light keeps the fire alive. Warm Standby is already dressed for work. Multi-site Active-Active has two offices open simultaneously.
